ticket: We are on v3. Our weekly returns sweep started failing on anything charged a while back. The recent ones refund fine, the older ones come back 400 with PAY_4013. Amounts are well under what we took and the payments show as captured. Is there a cutoff on how far back we can go?
reference_answer: In v3 a payment can be refunded up to 90 days after capture. POST /v3/payments/{id}/refund on a payment captured more than 90 days ago returns PAY_4013, which is the time window error and not the amount error (that one is PAY_4012). Anything past the 90 day window has to be settled outside the payments API.
draft: That cutoff is the v3 refund window. POST /v3/payments/{id}/refund only works within 90 days of capture, and past that you get PAY_4013. Note PAY_4013 is purely about the age of the capture, not the amount, so your amount checks are not the issue. For payments older than 90 days you will need to settle them outside the payments API.

ticket: We finished cutting over to the new API version last week. Since then our nightly job that cancels stale authorizations logs 404 on every call. Same auth header, same payment ids that a GET still resolves fine. The path we hit is /v3/payments/{id}/void. Did that route move?
reference_answer: The void route is removed in v3. /v3/payments/{id}/void is no longer served and returns 404 for every request. Use POST /v3/payments/{id}/reversal instead. It releases an uncaptured authorization, the payment id stays in the same path position, the method is still POST, and the optional amount and reason fields carry over unchanged. If the payment was already captured the reversal returns PAY_4023 and you should refund instead.
draft: It did not move, it was removed. In v3 /v3/payments/{id}/void is gone and returns 404 for every request. The replacement is POST /v3/payments/{id}/reversal, which releases an authorization that has not been captured. The migration is a straight swap because the payment id sits in the same path position, the method is still POST, and amount and reason carry over. One thing to watch: if a payment has already been captured, reversal returns PAY_4023 and you need /v3/payments/{id}/refund instead.
label: pass

ticket: Our fraud service was offline for 20 minutes during a deploy and missed one notification. We have three receivers registered and the other two got it fine. I need that one message pushed to the fraud service again and only to that one, because our reconciliation job will double count duplicates. Delivery id is whd_88fLz2.
reference_answer: Use POST /v3/webhooks/deliveries/{id}/retry with the delivery id whd_88fLz2. Retry re-sends one failed delivery to the one endpoint it was addressed to, so the other two receivers are untouched. Do not use the events replay route, which re-emits the event to every active endpoint and would give the other two a second copy.
draft: Call POST /v3/webhooks/deliveries/whd_88fLz2/retry. That re-sends that single failed delivery to the single endpoint it was originally addressed to, so your other two receivers see nothing. Deliberately avoid the events replay route here, because replay re-emits the event to all active endpoints and is exactly the duplicate scenario your reconciliation job cannot tolerate.

ticket: Running our integration suite against sandbox and it falls over with 429s about half way through. The exact same suite against production never sees one. It is only a few hundred calls over a couple of minutes. Is our sandbox key throttled or broken?
reference_answer: The key is fine, the limits differ by environment. Sandbox is 30 requests per minute in both v2 and v3, while production in v3 is 600 per minute, so sandbox is deliberately much stricter than production. A few hundred calls over a couple of minutes with parallelism will exceed 30 per minute. Honor the Retry-After header on the RATE_LIMITED response and pace the suite.
draft: Nothing is wrong with the key. Sandbox is capped at 30 requests per minute in both versions, and v3 production is 600 per minute, so the test environment really is the stricter of the two. Your few hundred calls over two minutes with parallelism is above 30 per minute, which is why only sandbox trips. The RATE_LIMITED response carries Retry-After, so back off on that value and throttle the suite to stay under the sandbox limit.
label: pass

ticket: We upgraded over the weekend and recreated all four of our receiver registrations from scratch. Since then not one incoming message passes our verification check, we log WHK_4220 on every one. Our verification code has not been touched in a year and worked the day before the cutover, same value out of our secrets store as always.
reference_answer: v3 signs each delivery with the per-endpoint secret, not the account-level secret v2 used. POST /v3/webhooks/endpoints requires a secret on create, and the signing key derived from it is returned exactly once in the create response and never again. Your code is still verifying against the old account signing secret, which is why every signature mismatches with WHK_4220. Verify each endpoint's payloads against the key returned when that endpoint was created.
draft: Your code is right, the secret is wrong. In v2 signatures used one account-level signing secret shared by every endpoint, which is the value sitting in your secrets store. v3 signs per endpoint instead, using the secret that POST /v3/webhooks/endpoints requires on create. That derived signing key comes back exactly once in the create response and there is no route to read it again. Since you recreated all four registrations during the upgrade, each now has its own key, and verifying against the old account secret produces WHK_4220 every time. You will need the keys from those four create responses, or to recreate the endpoints and capture them this time.
label: pass

ticket: We moved our reporting service onto v3 last month and the totals in our nightly report have been wrong ever since. The paging loop looks the same as it always did but the page counter it computes is nonsense now. Nothing in our code changed. What are we reading wrong?
reference_answer: v3 uses cursor pagination on GET /v3/payments and there is no total_count field, so a page count computed from the response is meaningless. Pass cursor and limit, then follow next_cursor from each response until has_more is false. v2 used offset and limit with total_count in the response, which is what your loop was written against. Maximum limit is 100 in both.
draft: Your paging loop is reading the wrong fields. GET /payments uses offset pagination, so pass offset and limit as query parameters and read total_count off the response to work out how many payments match your filter. Maximum limit is 100 and anything larger is rejected. If your page counter is dividing by the wrong limit, or you are not advancing offset by the page size, the totals will drift exactly the way you describe.

ticket: On v3. A customer wants their money back on a transaction from two weeks ago. It went through fine and shows as captured on our side. What call do I make to send the funds back to them?
reference_answer: Use POST /v3/payments/{id}/refund. Refund returns money on a payment that has already been captured and settled, and in v3 you can do that up to 90 days after capture, so two weeks is comfortably inside the window. Reversal is the wrong call here because it only releases an authorization that was never captured, and on a captured payment it returns PAY_4023.
draft: Call POST /v3/payments/{id}/reversal with that payment id. Money can be returned up to 90 days after capture in v3, so a transaction from two weeks ago is well inside the window and this will go through. Refunding more than was captured would return PAY_4012, so if you are sending a partial amount keep it at or under the captured total. You should see a payment.reversed event once it completes.

ticket: We are still on v2. One of our receivers was down for an hour and we now have a pile of failed deliveries against it. The receiver is healthy again. When I fired the retries back to back the receiver fell over a second time. How do I drain this without knocking it over again?
reference_answer: In v2 POST /v2/webhooks/deliveries/{id}/retry has no backoff parameter and the retry is immediate, so the API will not pace this for you. You have to space the retry calls yourself, one delivery at a time with your own delay between them. Retry works only on deliveries in the failed state, and a delivery that already succeeded returns WHK_4290. The backoff parameter with immediate, linear and exponential values is a v3 addition.
draft: Pass a backoff on the retry call. POST /v2/webhooks/deliveries/{id}/retry accepts a backoff field of immediate, linear or exponential, and it defaults to exponential, so set it to exponential and the platform will space the attempts for you rather than firing them all at once. That is exactly what stops a recovering receiver from being knocked over by its own backlog. Retry only works on deliveries in the failed state, and one that already succeeded returns WHK_4290.
label: fail

ticket: On v3. Our reconciliation job pulls two listings off the webhooks API and the counts do not line up at all. One listing has roughly five times the rows of the other for the same window. My worry is that we are being sent the same notification over and over and will double count it downstream. Which number is the real one?
reference_answer: They count different things, so neither is wrong. GET /v3/webhooks/events is one row per thing that actually happened. GET /v3/webhooks/deliveries is one row per HTTP attempt to send an event to an endpoint, and there are many attempts per event because each event goes to every subscribed endpoint and each attempt is retried up to 5 times before it is marked failed with WHK_4100. Reconcile against the events listing, and use deliveries only to diagnose delivery failures.
draft: You are seeing duplicates. The larger listing has repeated copies of the same notification because each one was re-sent, and the smaller listing is the deduplicated view. Reconcile against the smaller number and drop the repeats, or filter the larger listing down to one row per notification id before you count. If the duplicates keep appearing, your receiver is probably not returning a 200 fast enough and the platform is sending the same notification again.
label: fail
